analytic.title: Clockwerk: A Predictable and Efficient Extension of Logical Execution Time Model

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Real-time systems focus on achieving fast response time, which, however, is usually accompanied by sacrificing the predictability. The Logical Execution Time (LET) model achieves I/O-predictability by fixing the timing of reading inputs and writing outputs. However, LET lacks the mechanism to react to aperiodic requests which have frequently been used in soft real-time applications. To improve aperiodic responsiveness as well as obtain predictability, in this paper, we present a component-based LET extension-Clockwerk. Clockwerk introduces the concept of Servant as basic components to make both communication and computation parts of periodic tasks predictable. By combining the LET model with the aperiodic server, Clockwerk achieves the improvement of aperiodic responsiveness. Consequently, our proposal can reduce the complexity of schedulability analysis on periodic tasks to polynomial time, and preliminary simulation results show that it also achieves an aperiodic responsiveness speedup of 4.1X-6.5X compared with existing work.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: Real-time systems have been traditionally developed by focusing on achieving fast response times. The growing of such systems are subject to the optimization for processor utilization and average-case execution time. However, higher software complexity with optimization techniques, such as multi-threads programming and advanced architecture techniques, always cause non-determinism yielding increasingly validation costs. Thus, for one thing, real-time systems are supposed to be predictable to make themselves certifiable (i.e., they are easy to be validated). The predictability here refers to the deterministic execution of an application, i.e., given a particular set of inputs, the application will always produce the same set of outputs. For another, requirements for real-time systems to be reactive (i.e., they can always react to aperiodic stimuli) should be satisfied without the erosion on the foundation of the system predictability.

The Logical Execution Time (LET) model [1], first introduced by Giotto [2], achieves predictability by forcing the system to interact with environments at the designated time instant. Different to traditional programming models, such as the Bounded Execution Time (BET) and Zero Execution Time (ZET) overviewed in [1], the LET specifies a logical execution time (let) for each periodic task, regardless of its physical computational execution. Thus, LET-based tasks possess I/O-predictability by fixing the instant to read inputs and write outputs at the beginning and end of task let respectively. xGiotto [3] extends the LET with event-Figure 1. Architecture of Clockwerk driven mechanism to react to aperiodic requests. However, postponement and even abandonment of aperiodic requests severely jeopardize the aperiodic responsiveness of systems. Moreover, schedulability analysis on xGiotto programs requires EXPTIME which makes it impractical.

In this research, we propose a LET extension -Clockwerk combining the LET with Servants and aperiodic server to enhance the aperiodic responsiveness of systems without the erosion on the system predictability.

div.head: II. THE CLOCKWERK DESIGN 1) Periodic Activities:
div.p: A Clockwerk-based program is composed of modes, tasks and Servants, as shown in Fig. 1. Each Mode has a period which equals to the least common multiple of periods of its containing tasks. A mode can switch to another mode when corresponding mode switch condition is satisfied. Each task is assigned with a let which equals to the task period. A periodic task can be divided into non-preemptive Servants. Each Servant connects with others through communication channels established in terms of data dependencies among Servants. Clockwerk programs designate each Servant with an time slot which is greater than or equals to their worst-case execution time (wcet). Servants execute non-preemptively during the slot. Servants comprise I-Servants, C-Servants and O-Servants, for reading inputs, processing data and writing outputs respectively.

Timing behaviors of Servants represent timing behaviors of systems. To keep consistent with the semantics of LET, I-Servants (O-Servants) are scheduled at the start (end) of the task let, while C-Servants execute during the let. The concept of Unit is introduced to isolate executions of C-Servants and I/O-Servants to keep I/O-behaviors execute in time. The Unit has a period which equals to the greatest common divisor of periodic tasks. Each Unit is further subdivided into three duration for scheduling I-Servants, C-Servants, and O-Servants respectively. Servants are scheduled in a determinate order in each duration. As for C-Servants, in each Unit, the timing analysis performs to decide whether the C-Servant can be scheduled in current Unit. If the specified time slot of the C-Servants is greater than the remainder of time interval of current Unit, the rest of unscheduled C-Servants are deferred to be scheduled in subsequent Units. Otherwise, C-Servant executes by determined timing behaviors generated by causality relations, priorities and unique ids (This is not discussed here due to the limitation of length). Benefit from the determinism, timing behaviors of Clockwerk become predictable on the basis of the time-triggered mechanism [2] at system level. All Servants have to be scheduled before their Latest Release Time (LRT), which are generated by determinate timing behaviors, for meeting time constraints.

Analysis: schedulability analysis on a Clockwerk program completes for only O(NM) instead of EXPTIME. Where the M is the number of modes in the program, and N is the number of Servant invocations in the mode. Specifically, periodic tasks can be schedulable if all their containing Servants execute before the end of their let. It can be done through searching the scheduling table which contains predetermined timing behaviors for O(N ) time. Thus, the analysis on a Clockwerk-based program consisting of M modes completes for O(NM).

2) Aperiodic Activities: Aperiodic tasks managed by the aperiodic server execute in terms of priority exchange policy to take full advantage of available processing time. The aperiodic server in Clockwerk is based on the priority exchange (PE) algorithm [4]. PE main considers saving the execution time allocated for the aperiodic server if, upon the invocation of the server, no aperiodic requests are pending. The server schedules aperiodic tasks triggered by aperiodic requests, such as button pushing signals and GIPO signals, in a FIFO approach. The aperiodic server acts as a periodic task whose period T S equals to the period of the current mode. The server capacity C S is replenished to T Sslot each time when the system enters a new mode period. Where slot denotes the sum of designated time slots of Servants invocations in the mode. The capacity is consumed when the server runs. Specifically, the following happens:

• If no aperiodic task is pending, unscheduled C-Servants (I/O-servants must be scheduled at the start/end of task let) of released tasks start running for saving aperiodic capacity. The system enters the idle state while all C-Servants in current Unit finish. • If aperiodic tasks are pending, the aperiodic server will become the highest priority task after the execution of the running Servant, or when no Servant is running. A Servant forced to be released at its LRT will preempt the execution of the running aperiodic server. New arrival aperiodic requests are therefore deferred. Simulation: Simulations were conducted by using M/M/1 queuing analysis for both Clockwerk and xGiotto. As shown in Fig. 2, three periodic tasks set loads a utilization of 40%, 60%, 80% to simulate multi-rate task combinations paradigm. A set of four periodic tasks with wcets ranges from 5 to 100 time units were selected. By defining periods of tasks to 300 or 900 time units, we can get the mode period which equals to 900 time units, and the Unit period which equals to 300 time units. For each periodic load simulation, corresponding aperiodic loads are set to be 58%, 38%, 18% to reach total 98% processor utilization (2% kernel overheads). Aperiodic mean service times are obtained by 1%, 2%, and 5% of the server period which is identical to the mode period. Aperiodic task arrival times are modeled using a Poisson arrival process, and aperiodic task service times are modeled using exponential distribution. Simulation results show that the aperiodic responsiveness of Clockwerk achieves an average response time speedup of 4.1X-6.5X compared with xGiotto.

Therefore, our proposal can enhance the aperiodic responsiveness as well as maintain predictability of LET. Future work comprising constructing efficient runtime system and effective programming framework worth further researching.
